data.title: Pityriasis rubra pilaris — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 8 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis rubra pilaris** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP)?**
- Rare chronic papulosquamous disorder with follicular keratotic papules, orange-red scaly plaques with islands of sparing, and palmoplantar keratoderma; can progress to erythroderma
- Bimodal age: childhood and adults (5th–6th decade)

**Q2. Classify PRP (Griffiths).**
- Type I — classic adult (commonest ~50%): starts on head/upper trunk → spreads caudally to erythroderma with islands of sparing; resolves in ~80% within 3 years
- Type II — atypical adult: ichthyosiform lower-leg scaling, alopecia, eczematous areas, long duration (20 years)
- Type III — classic juvenile: like type I, resolves in 1–2 years
- Type IV — circumscribed juvenile: knees and elbows plaques (commonest in children), variable course
- Type V — atypical juvenile: familial, early onset, scleroderma-like hands, chronic; CARD14 gain-of-function
- Type VI — HIV-associated: with acne conglobata, hidradenitis, lichen spinulosus; responds to ART

**Q3. Describe the clinical features of classic adult PRP.**
- Follicular hyperkeratotic papules ('nutmeg-grater' feel) especially on the dorsa of proximal phalanges (knuckles), elbows, knees
- Coalescing salmon/orange-red plaques with fine scale spreading cephalocaudally; well-defined islands of normal skin ('nappes claires')
- Orange-red waxy palmoplantar keratoderma ('keratodermic sandal')
- Scalp: diffuse branny scaling; face: red, ectropion; nails: yellow-brown discolouration, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages (no pits)

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Unknown in most; abnormal keratinisation, vitamin A metabolism (low retinol-binding protein — old theory), IL-23/Th17 axis (rationale for IL-17/23 biologics), CARD14 mutations in familial type V; triggers — infections, UV, drugs, malignancy (paraneoplastic in elderly)

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in horizontal and vertical directions — chequerboard pattern; follicular plugging with 'shoulder parakeratosis', thick granular layer, broad short rete ridges, sparse perivascular infiltrate; acantholysis (focal) can occur
- Distinguish from psoriasis: no Munro microabscesses, no thinning of suprapapillary plate, granular layer preserved

**Q6. Differentiate PRP from psoriasis.**
- PRP: orange-red colour, follicular papules on knuckles, islands of sparing, waxy orange palmoplantar keratoderma, fine scale, no nail pits, no Auspitz sign, histology chequerboard
- Psoriasis: red with silvery scale, plaques on extensors, pits/oil-drop nails, Auspitz sign, PsA, Munro microabscesses

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Topical: emollients, keratolytics (urea, salicylic acid, lactic acid), topical steroids, calcipotriol
- Systemic first line: oral retinoids — isotretinoin 0.5–1 mg/kg/day or acitretin 0.5–0.75 mg/kg/day for 4–6 months
- Methotrexate 10–25 mg weekly (alone or with retinoid), cyclosporine, azathioprine
- Biologics for refractory: TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab), IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), IL-23 inhibitors
- Phototherapy may aggravate (photosensitivity) — use with caution; vitamin A historically
- Treat erythroderma complications; HIV testing in atypical cases

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Type I and III often remit within 3 years; types II, V chronic; erythrodermic disease needs intensive care

## Quick spotter facts
- Islands of sparing + orange keratoderma + follicular knuckle papules — PRP
- Chequerboard ortho/parakeratosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pityriasis rubra pilaris). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
